en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Ji of Daci’en Monastery. 1.
Preface (Volume 1, from the beginning to the end). To examine this in detail: the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is as still as space, opening the pivot of the profound within non-duality;

expedient means (*upāya*) give birth to the Way, unfolding the wondrous jewels within the absence of three. Thus, some manifest the vast and grand design, nobly declining the karmic legacy of the Golden Wheel [of sovereignty].

Some secretly opened the way for the ultimate, while others humbly assisted the legacy of the Jade璞 (purity); all desired to clear away the burning heat with the wise rain and wash away the channels of drowning with the ferry of compassion. They pointed toward the nine realms to realize the ten voids, and invoked the eight liberations to unfold the seven factors of enlightenment. How sublime and magnificent! It is difficult to find a name for it.
This present sutra contains the great void of myriad tenets and binds the celestial marsh of all expedient means;

its principle exhausts the treasury of both the ultimate and the conventional, while its traces transcend the realm of mind and speech. Its divine mechanism is profound and unfathomable, its pure virtue serene and inconceivable;
it shifts billions of worlds with a single step and maneuvers the three thousandfold world-system within the palm of its hand.

The universe is encompassed within a single canopy, revealing the precarious floating of the dust-motes and mountains; the *cubit-room* (*zhàngshì*) subsumes the eight directions, illuminating the site of truth with eternal purity.
The sublime heights are contained within a hair-tip or a mustard seed, such that objects are equalized whether large or small;
the vast ocean is poured into a puddle in a hoofprint, such that breadth and narrowness are interwoven as one. Thus, the secret bolt of the profound gateway is opened, and [the world] is shifted...

The Way of the Garden of Enlightenment has been attained; like a bull emerging from a dilapidated house or an elephant crossing the river of the ocean, it has caused jade tablets to be sent westward and golden forms to shine eastward.
Competing in appreciation for the One Truth, it has already passed through six translations.
Subsequently, as the Chinese and Indian languages were vastly separated and their phonetic systems divergent, some merely imitated the literal phrasing while distilling away the profound essence.

The Great Master [Xuanzang] illuminated the Middle Way amidst the phases of the moon of practice and mirrored the Perfect Teaching within the terrace of the mind; he repaired the severed threads to benefit future generations and mended the collapsing framework to establish a precedent for those who came before. He refined what was right and wrong and deliberated upon terminology and meaning, translating this sutra once again in accordance with the true path.

The Preface to the First Chapter, "Introduction," of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*: With a golden voice issuing from a golden mouth and jade characters proclaimed from a jade banner, he awakens the multitudes of the hearing and proclaims the teaching. His Way merges with the True Sovereign (*zhenzai*), and his activity embodies the numinous mechanism of *dāna*. He conceals his purple sleeves to manifest his hidden majesty and pairs with the profound Confucian to radiate his brilliance. Whether through skillful means or ultimate reality, he manifests illness to expound the Great Vehicle; now hidden and now revealed, he employs dialogue to illuminate his essential nature and mandate. Among the ten sons of renowned fame, all were surpassed in rhetoric and the Way; as the one person who received the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), his majestic presence was but a faint shadow. Having purified his holy conduct (*brahmacarya*) and solemnized the divine ritual, his elegant reputation spread afar, and he was named Vimalakīrti.
"Sūtra" means "to thread through" and "to encompass": it threads through two principles without deficiency and encompasses the four modes of birth without failure.
"Preface" (xu) means "source" and "beginning": it sets forth the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching and the gradual commencement of its composition.

"Chapter" (*pin*) means category or distinction; it refers to the classification of profound principles and the systematic arrangement of subtle methods, delineating categories to make them manifest, which is why they are termed "chapters.
This scripture consists of six fascicles and contains a total of fourteen chapters.
Now, this Jianchu era is thus called the first.
Sūtra: Thus have I heard.
Commentary says:
Now, in explaining this sutra, it shall be analyzed by means of six sections:
first, the causes for the arising of the sutra;
second, the core tenets of the sutra.
Third, clarifying the essential nature of the sūtra;
fourth, describing the differences among the sūtras;
fifth, identifying the origins of the chapters and sections.
Sixth, the explanation of the meaning of the main text. Regarding the first, the causes for the arising of the sutra, there are briefly five kinds:

first, to cause sentient beings to give rise to aspiration and revulsion; second, to cause those of the two vehicles to have that which to adopt and that which to reject; third, to manifest the internal and external cultivation of bodhisattvas; fourth, to manifest the majestic power and great virtue of the Tathāgata; and fifth, because the faculties of the assembly at that time were mature and ready to hear it.

First, regarding the purpose of causing sentient beings to give rise to aspiration and revulsion: looking upward at the Buddha’s manifestations for the benefit of living beings, there are no more than two kinds:
first, manifesting his physical body; second, preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding the bodies of all Buddhas, they are fundamentally non-dual.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "If one can reckon that the Three Jewels are eternally abiding and identical to the ultimate truth, this is the most supreme and sublime vow of all Buddhas."
According to what is appropriate for beings to hear and see, there are three divisions:
first, the Dharma-body, which is the true principle free from delusion;
second, the Reward-body, which is the actual wisdom that realizes the truth.
The third is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which is the provisional substance that responds to sentient beings.
Thus, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "The self-nature body, the enjoyment body, and the transformation body function with distinct differences."
"In the past, one was shrouded by falsehood; worldly affairs obscured the mind and ignorance arose.
Now, by relying on the True Dharma for cultivation, the Correct Principle becomes manifest and the karmic reward emerges.
Indeed, the Principle is the foundation of the path to awakening; when its state is revealed, it is designated as the Dharmakāya."
Recompense is the precursor to sagely virtue; when practice is perfected, it accords with the essence of recompense.
As for the subtle principle—that which those of middling capacity have not yet realized—is the Buddha-nature and the Dharma-body.
Those of middling capacity are bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Because bodhisattvas of the ten stages have not yet clearly realized the Buddha-nature and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the "Bodhisattva Stage" (*Bodhisattvabhūmi*) states: "The objects appearing to a bodhisattva of the tenth stage are like a clear-sighted person looking through a thin veil."
Furthermore, the *Vipaśyanā-bimba-śāstra* also states: "The Dharma-body of all Buddhas can be known only by Buddhas and by Buddhas.
Since those of middling capacity have not yet attained realization, those of inferior capacity certainly do not know it.
Those of superior wisdom and those of inferior folly do not know the superior wisdom; the "superior wisdom" refers to the Buddha’s wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The "inferior fools" refer to those of the two vehicles and ordinary worldlings.
These individuals of the two vehicles and ordinary worldlings are unable to know the true wisdom of the Buddha.

Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Even if the entire world were filled with beings like Śāriputra, and they were to exhaust their thoughts to measure it together, they could not know the Buddha’s wisdom."
The subsequent passages are not yet known, and even those of middling capacity have not yet understood them.

Therefore, he manifests transformational bodies by adapting to the capacities of beings, dividing his body into ten billion forms to transform those of the Two Vehicles and ordinary worldlings; this is the wondrous function of the *nirmāṇakāya*. He appears as a manifest realization of awakening and manifests the wondrous Great Body to accommodate the spiritual potential of living beings, transforming the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages; this is the wondrous function of the *parasaṃbhogakāya*.
The empty walls naturally manifest painted colors, vast and boundlessly luminous; the poured water reflects the brilliance of crystal, its radiance reaching its limit.
The provisional and ultimate aspects of the Buddha-body may be clearly understood through these analogies.

Therefore, the subsequent scripture says: "The assembled multitude gazed upon the Great Muni, and there was none whose mind did not give rise to pure faith; each saw the World-Honored One standing before them—this is the unique characteristic (āveṇika-lakṣaṇa) of the Tathāgata."

Since the body is without distinction, the three [vehicles] are taught according to what is appropriate; since the Dharma is without discrepancy, it abides in accordance with capacities to form the four [noble truths]. It is like a wish-fulfilling jewel that rains down treasures according to one's requests, or like the drum of the Heavenly Lord that emits sound in response to a thought.
The Dharma is of four kinds:
first, teaching; second, principle; third, practice; and fourth, fruition.
Although the dharmas differ in myriad ways, they do not exceed these four.
That which the intellect understands through verbal expression is called "teaching" (dharma).
That which is expressed by the teaching is termed "principle" (tattva).
Cultivating practice in accordance with that principle constitutes "conduct" (caryā).
That which is realized through cultivation is designated as the "fruit.
Yet these four types are each non-dual; they differ according to conditions but are universally accessible to all three vehicles.

Therefore, the sutra below states: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own capacity; they all receive its benefit and obtain its advantage—this is the unique characteristic of the Tathāgata."

This teaching is uniform, yet it accommodates three capacities; it is like the *Lotus Sūtra*, where a single rain universally moistens the three vehicles and the three types of grasses, while the two sages and two trees grow at different rates. Thus, while the teaching is the same, the capacities differ, resulting in the formation of the three vehicles.

This sutra further states: "When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, some feel fear, some feel joy, some develop weary detachment, and some sever their doubts; this is the unique characteristic of the Tathāgata."
This also follows the same principle:

while the nature of the river remains undifferentiated, there are distinctions in how the rabbit, horse, and elephant cross it according to their respective capacities. *Ratnagotravibhāga* states that the nature of the river is without difference, yet there are differences in the three crossings of the rabbit, horse, and elephant.
This illustrates how the principle remains the same while the manifestations differ, thereby establishing the doctrine of the Three Vehicles.

In the *Lotus Sūtra*, the garments, baskets, tables, and the single gate are all identical; although the means of exit differ, they are equal in their ability to escape all calamities and serve as the cause for obtaining the ox-carts.

The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* further states: "The abiding of the True Dharma, the extinction of the True Dharma, the Prātimokṣa, the Vinaya, leaving the household life, and receiving full ordination—these six dharmas constitute the Mahāyāna."

Therefore, in the various sūtras and śāstras of the two piṭakas, "abiding" (sthiti) is designated as "good covering" (saṃvara), and "cessation" (nirodha) is designated as "removal of obstacles" (āvaraṇa-vinodana).

Within the precepts, the abbreviated root text is called the Prātimokṣa, while the extensive disciplinary root text is called the Vinaya; these constitute the Dharma of the Three Piṭakas that is to be studied.

Those who are able to study this are called "those who have left the household life" (pravrajita); they receive the full precepts (upasampadā) of the two vehicles, and when person and dharma are combined, these constitute the six bases.
Since it is stated that all are taught for the sake of the Mahāyāna, we know that the minor studies serve as the great cause for its realization.
This is because while their practice is the same, their cultivation differs; due to the distinction between the sudden and the gradual, the karma of the three vehicles is established.

Furthermore, the *Lotus Sūtra* states that the "transformed city" was taught midway as a place of rest, thus speaking of two [vehicles], and that the three carts were first used as inducements, but later the ox-carts were bestowed equally.

This is because while the fruit is the same, there are differences in its provisional establishment; due to the distinction between the nominal and the substantial, the fruits of the three vehicles are realized.
Thus, one should know that the dharmatā of all phenomena taught is without differentiation, yet it manifests in various ways according to external conditions.
There are briefly five reasons why this sūtra was composed; how then can it be known that it causes sentient beings to give rise to delight and aversion?
There are two kinds of delight and aversion:
first, internal delight and aversion; second, external delight and aversion.
Regarding "internal joy and aversion": "aversion" refers to aversion toward the body of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), while "joy" refers to joy in the body of a future Buddha.
The "Expedient Means" chapter states: "At that time, Vimalakīrti, through great skillful means, manifested himself as being ill."
Because of his illness, thousands of kings, ministers, elders, and householders all went to inquire after him.
At that time, Vimalakīrti extensively expounded the Dharma for them.
He said:
"O virtuous ones!
This body, composed of the four great elements, is impermanent, lacks strength, is without solidity or power, is subject to rapid decay, and cannot be relied upon."
Afflicted by suffering, a vessel for manifold diseases, fraught with many calamities, and subject to decay—O virtuous ones!
Such a body as this is not to be relied upon by those who are wise; and so on, in detail, until: O virtuous ones!
One should cultivate revulsion toward such a body as this, and one should give rise to joyful aspiration for the body of a Tathāgata.

The body of a Tathāgata is that which is collectively accumulated from immeasurable wholesome dharmas; it arises from the cultivation of immeasurable superior merit and wisdom; it arises from ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—and so forth, as extensively explained. O virtuous ones!
The body of the Tathāgata possesses such merit; you all should resolve to seek its realization.
If you wish to attain such a body and to pacify the illnesses of all sentient beings, you must give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Thus, he dispels the mind of weariness and suffering, cuts off the root of suffering, causes one to rejoice in the Buddha-body, and practice the causes of Buddhahood.
Therefore, we know that he manifested illness to display the inconceivable, desiring to arouse within sentient beings both joy and revulsion.

Furthermore, when the task of extolling [the Buddha's virtues] was completed and they were about to proceed to the Āmra Grove, the great assembly surrounding the Buddha all appeared golden in color. Those who understood the principles of delighting in and loathing [samsara] knew that their hearts would surely bear fruit in the future.
Regarding those outside [the assembly], "loathing" refers to King Saṃjīva (the King of Impurity), while "delighting" refers to the Land of Purity.
This sutra describes two kinds of pure lands:
first, those manifested by sages of this world, and second, those manifested by sages of other worlds.
There are likewise two kinds of defiled lands:
One manifestation of a sentient being and one manifestation of Śākyamuni.
Examining the beginning and end of the discourse throughout the text, the lands upon which they rely consist of two defiled and two pure realms.

Initially, the Buddha was in the Āmra Garden at Vaiśālī, extensively expounding the sublime Dharma for the fourfold assembly. When Ratnākara offered a parasol and questioned the Buddha regarding the nature of phenomena, the Buddha manifested supernatural powers by merging the parasols to answer his inquiry; however, he did not yet clarify the distinct meanings concerning the various lands and their ordinary abodes.
Kṣetra told Ratnākara:
"If you wish to diligently cultivate the purification of a Buddha-field, you must first employ skillful means to purify your own mind.
Then, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, Śāriputra suddenly had this thought:

"If it is the case that when a bodhisattva’s mind is pure, the buddha-field is purified, then let it not be that when I practiced as a bodhisattva, my mind was not purified, such that this land is now mixed with impurities."
The Buddha questioned him with an incomparable parable, yet Śāriputra remained unaware. Holding his topknot, he spoke at length, seeking a way to awaken.

The World-Honored One dispelled the doubts of the assembly; sometimes he pressed down upon the great trichiliocosm, declaring it transformed into a magnificent array of precious jewels, whereupon Śāriputra finally praised this rare sight.
When the five hundred youths of the Jewel Nature had realized non-arising, eighty-four thousand sentient beings all heard it and gave rise to the wisdom of awakening.
Once his work of transformation was complete and the assembly was ready, the Buddha withdrew his supernormal powers, and the world returned to its former state.

Later, the Buddha dispatched Mañjuśrī to inquire after Vimalakīrti’s illness. Once their dialogue was concluded and he was about to depart for the Āmrapālī grove, the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice" demonstrates that his manifestation is inconceivable:

the Āmrapālī grove suddenly becomes vast and expansive. Yet, until the sutra has finished being preached, there is no further mention of it returning to its former state of filth; this reveals the method of loathing impurity and delighting in purity, which must ultimately result in complete adornment and purification.
In the first three [cases], the defiled lands appear; in the second and fourth, the pure realms are transformed.
In the first, our World-Honored One himself transforms the pure land; subsequently, Vimalakīrti and Mañjuśrī again separate from the defiled regions.
Therefore, it is said that this Pure Land is a transformation of this very Sage, for both the Buddha and Vimalakīrti are one and the same Sage.
Regarding the manifestations of other sages, there are two types:

first, as described in the "Chapter on the Fragrant Terrace," when Śāriputra was thinking of food, Vimalakīrti then manifested supernatural powers; thirty-two *gaṅgā*-sands of Buddha-worlds away from here in the upward direction, there is a Buddha-world named Wondrous Fragrance (*Gandhavatī*), where the Buddha is titled Supreme Fragrant Terrace (*Gandhottamakūṭa*).
That realm is entirely composed of fragrance;
there are no followers of the two vehicles at all, but only pure great bodhisattvas.

At that time, this great assembly all beheld the Buddha’s land and its various features; one thousand sentient beings all resolved their minds upon Bodhi, and ten thousand bodhisattvas simultaneously realized the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
In the second chapter, "Contemplating the Tathāgata," those of lower capacity do not understand the higher station, and the mind of Śāriputra suddenly gave rise to doubt:
"From where has this Vimalakīrti come here?"
The Buddha said, "In the world-system of Abhirati there is the Tathāgata Akṣobhya; he has come here for the sake of delivering these sentient beings.
The great assembly felt a deep yearning and desired to see the bodhisattvas and the pure buddha-field adorned with the merits of Abhirati.
Then Vimalakīrti plucked that world away and placed it in the palm of his right hand—like a potter’s wheel or a string of flowers—and brought it into this world to show it to the great assembly.
Although these two realms were thus intermingled, each person saw their own dwelling as no different from before.
The Buddha addressed the great assembly:
"Those who wish to attain such a magnificent buddha-field should all follow and learn from the original practices cultivated by the Tathāgata Akṣobhya."

At that time, there were eighty-four nayutas of humans, devas, and others in this land who all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and vowed to be born in that realm; the World-Honored One prophesied that they would all indeed be born there.
These two are said to be manifested for others by the noble ones, because both the Fragrant Terrace and the Immovable World are [realms] for others and the noble ones.

They cause one to weary of the defiled land so that evil causes do not arise, and they lead one to delight in the pure direction so as to cultivate pure karma. Through this, the land is transformed to manifest the inconceivable, desiring to inspire in sentient beings external feelings of aspiration and weariness.
When ordinary beings hear the Dharma and practice it, they must take joy and revulsion as their foundation.
Within the sutras, there are two types of pure lands manifested by this Sage:
first, those manifested by Śākyamuni himself; second, those manifested in anticipation of the arrival of the one of wondrous virtue, Mañjuśrī.
The pure lands manifested through transformation are also of two kinds:
first, the wondrous fragrance observed from afar; second, the wondrous joy beheld nearby.
The defiled lands are likewise of two kinds:
First, the transformation of a single sentient being; second, the transformation of Śākyamuni.
Therefore, the "Introduction Chapter" states: "He addressed Śāriputra:
'My Buddha-land is eternally pure just like this.'"
It is for the sake of maturing inferior sentient beings that he manifests this land as being filled with immeasurable faults and impurities.
It is, for example, like the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven who eat from a single precious vessel; yet, according to what their respective karma has summoned, the food they receive differs.
"Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Immeasurable sentient beings are born in a single buddha-field, yet what they perceive differs according to the purity or impurity of their own minds.
For this reason, while the Pure Land is fundamentally the land of the Noble Ones, through his supernatural power, the Buddha causes other inferior sentient beings to likewise perceive it as pure.
Because these defiled realms are originally the lands of inferior sentient beings, they are also considered defiled when followed by noble ones (*ārya*).

Regarding these various bodies and lands—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), whether real or semblance, whether corresponding to the fruit or the perfection, and whether corresponding to ordinary persons or noble ones—the pure and impure transformations perceived by one's own consciousness or another consciousness should all be distinguished according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
This holy transformation and purification briefly has two conditions:
first, to dispel minor doubts; second, to awaken the minds of the multitude.

While the transformations and purifications of other sages are for all Tathāgatas to transform impurities, they are intended only for those of the Two Vehicles and the class of ordinary beings, not for Bodhisattvas.
Question:
For what reason did Śāriputra give rise to doubt regarding the Tathāgata’s transformation of his own pure land,
while when Vimalakīrti was about to arrive, Mañjuśrī preemptively transformed the Precious Quarter?
Answer:
To dispel doubts and eliminate afflictions, the Tathāgata himself transforms the pure realm;
to stir the sentiments of the multitude, Miaode (Wonderful Virtue) first transforms and adorns the land.
Question:
Why does the Pure Name not bring the Pure Land of Wondrous Fragrance?
[Yet] the Pure Name holds the Precious Quarter of Wonderful Joy within his palm.
Answer:
In the Land of Exquisite Fragrance, one must eat rice; although it is seen there, it is not brought [to this world].
In the Land of Supreme Joy, supernatural powers are manifested so that things may be seen, and they are also held within the palms.
The supernatural powers used for salvation and benefit employ manifold provisional means; why must they be sent together to be held, or made to be seen simultaneously?
Question:

Since the Buddha fundamentally saves living beings by establishing the benefits of joy and revulsion, why does he not also cause them to see the pure realm, rather than merely temporarily separating them from the defiled region?
Answer:
When the faculties are mature and conditions are required, one temporarily causes them to see the pure;
when conditions are not required and [the faculties] are not yet mature, one employs the method of manifesting the defiled.
Second, regarding "in order to cause those of the two vehicles who possess grasping and abandoning to [attain it]," there are two types of grasping and abandoning:
first, internal grasping and abandoning; second, external grasping and abandoning.
As for internal grasping and abandoning: "abandoning" refers to abandoning the mind of the two vehicles, and "grasping" refers to grasping the wisdom of the Mahāyāna.

There are two kinds of obstructions: first, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); second, the obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). The former obstructs nirvāṇa, while the latter obstructs bodhi. Śrāvakas sever the former;

having already transcended birth and death, they have attained nirvāṇa. However, they cannot sever the latter; they have not yet realized bodhi nor mastered all phenomena. Therefore, the dualistic mind of conceptualization still exists for those of the Two Vehicles.
By means of these inferior dharmas, that [wisdom] also matures non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
That which is accomplished by the Bodhisattva, through these superior dharmas, also matures.
Thus, the meaning of the path of adoption and rejection is made clear.
For this reason, Śāriputra sits in quietude with body and mind stilled; his every movement manifests dignified deportment, as he constantly dwells in the meditative absorption of cessation.
Maudgalyāyana preaches the Dharma to benefit the lay devotees, demonstrating that the Dharma transcends words—this alone is called true preaching.
Kāśyapa begged for alms by going from the poor to the wealthy, so as to equalize compassion and practice the destruction of attachments.
When Subhūti held his bowl and practiced begging in Śrāvastī, he transformed people’s houses into being equal in principle; only then could he accept them.

Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, preach and expound to the newly initiated students, transmitting to them the Great Dharma; do not, like the śrāvakas who shave their heads and follow the Buddha’s discernment of suffering and emptiness, use a mind of discrimination to speak of the Dharma of true reality.

The Unextinguished One, with the clear vision of the divine eye, beholds the great trichiliocosm; he simultaneously examines both existence and non-existence, yet it is only through the vision of meditative concentration that one attains full realization.

He rebuked two individuals for their attachment to worldly things and commanded them not to disturb their minds, for when the mind is defiled, transgression arises, and when the mind is pure, defilement is extinguished.
He took up the praise of the virtues of renunciation to entice that young boy, teaching him to abandon discrimination and attain the unconditioned; this was the benefit of his renunciation.
When the World-Honored One manifested illness, Ānanda, on this account, requested milk; [the Buddha] then spoke of the Buddha’s untainted body to cause him to abandon the views of the Two Vehicles.

I humbly observe that even when he encountered us in the past, he still exhorted us to abandon the mind of discrimination; how much more so now, when manifesting illness to expound the Great Vehicle—would he not praise the conferral of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom?
Therefore, in the "Chapter on Inquiring after Illness," when Śāriputra was about to go and inquire after his illness, Vimalakīrti first emptied his house.
This not only accords with the [teachings of] the Buddhas of the ten directions, but also manifests the emptying of all conceptual discrimination.

In the "Chapter on the Inconceivable," Śāriputra was moved by wonder at the couch; the Buddha rebuked him for seeking it for himself and commanded him to use it for the Dharma. Subsequently, he requested the throne of King Prabhūtaratna to provide a place of rest for both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, extensively expounding upon the inconceivable and declaring that this is not the realm of the two vehicles.
Kāśyapa led the way for those born blind, using himself as a metaphor for his own lack of understanding; the difficulty of comprehending this is inconceivable.
In the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings," when the celestial maidens scattered flowers, the Śrāvakas were immediately stained by them.
Śāriputra, because the flowers were not in accordance with the Dharma, exhausted his supernatural powers to remove them.
The goddess said, "These flowers are in accordance with the Dharma; it is the Venerable One himself who is not in accordance with the Dharma."
"Flowers have no discrimination, yet the Venerable One possesses it.

In the "Chapter on the Fragrant Terrace," Śāriputra, seeing that the time for his meal was approaching, thought of what he would eat; thus, regarding the food of the Fragrant Terrace, [the Buddha] exhorted him to abandon the mindset of a śrāvaka.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Through three kinds of refinement, one eliminates the obstacles in four areas.

When those of the two vehicles apply their mental attention, they distance themselves from doubt; yet as long as the mind possesses conceptual discrimination, it remains deluded regarding its object. Once discrimination is removed, one then merges with the true principle.
Therefore, those who possess conceptual discrimination have not yet harmonized with the subtlety of the True Doctrine and cannot realize Bodhi;
those who are free from conceptual discrimination ultimately accord with the ultimate of the Mysterious Gate and only then achieve Great Enlightenment.
Thus we know that he manifested illness to display the inconceivable, desiring to inspire within those of the Two Vehicles a sense of aspiration for liberation and revulsion toward saṃsāra.
Since the bodies of śrāvakas perish spontaneously, he spoke only of the mind of wisdom when discussing internal aspiration and revulsion.
When the discriminating mind ceases, delusive objects become empty;
once right wisdom has arisen, their true principle manifests.
Question:
Question: Since the multitude of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are so numerous, why is it that Śāriputra alone has repeatedly suffered defeat in debate?
Answer:
Although the great assembly of śrāvakas is vast, Śāriputra alone is preeminent.
Raising one's head to respond with praise, one knows that all others are surpassed.
Regarding "external joy and aversion": "aversion" refers to wearying detachment from the defiled land, while "joy" refers to rejoicing in the pure land.
There are three types of Buddha-lands:
First is the Dharma-nature land, the dwelling place of the Dharma-body, which is the principle of True Suchness;
second is the Enjoyment land, the dwelling place of the Reward-body, adorned with various jewels;
third is the Transformation land, the dwelling place of the Emanation-body, where purity and impurity are not fixed.
The details will be extensively analyzed in the subsequent text.

Although both Miaode (Subhūti) and Jingming (Vimalakīrti) transformed the Āmra grove to make it pure and universally alerted the great assembly of the time, why would this have been done solely for the sake of converting the śrāvakas?

Only when Upāli held his topknot and faced him did the World-Honored One press his foot down; the great trichiliocosm was transformed into purity, and immediately returned to its usual state. This was a transformation performed solely for the sake of the śrāvakas, in order to resolve the doubts of Śāriputra.
Although the great assembly saw this together, it should not be understood as being for the śrāvakas alone.
When Śāriputra alone gave rise to doubt at that time, these were therefore both called "manifestations.
This was the initial manifestation of the pure land, intended to inspire longing for the external [pure realm] and revulsion toward the current state in those of the two vehicles.
What appears subsequently pertains to all [beings].
Since the matters are identical to those mentioned above, they cannot be described in full detail.

Because the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is also pure; because the mind has defilements, the Buddha-field is also defiled. For this reason, the preceding discussion on delighting in or loathing, and accepting or rejecting, was spoken of in terms of both the internal and the external.

Third, to clarify the internal and external cultivation of bodhisattvas: although the specific practices cultivated by bodhisattvas are difficult to enumerate individually, they may be summarized and categorized briefly into no more than two types:
first, internal cultivation; second, external cultivation.
Internal cultivation refers to cultivating within oneself the merits for one's own benefit that are to be accomplished, with great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) and so forth as the primary factors.
External cultivation refers to cultivating externally the merits for the benefit of others that are to be accomplished, with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and so forth as the primary factors.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Although the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas, according to their respective inclinations, all pertain to both the categories of self-benefit and benefit for others—
since rescuing and delivering sentient beings is itself one's own benefit,
and since what one personally cultivates and advances toward is for the sake of sentient beings— they are designated according to whichever aspect is predominant."
The six pāramitās, the karma of the various marks and signs, the factors of enlightenment, and so forth, are called practices for one’s own benefit.
The six supernormal powers, the four immeasurables, the four means of attraction, and so forth, are called practices for the benefit of others.

Regarding the practitioner who acts for their own benefit, this sūtra’s "Introduction Chapter," in its praise of the bodhisattva’s virtues, states: "The majestic power of all Buddhas constantly sustains them; they well protect the city of the Dharma and are able to uphold the True Dharma, continuing the lineage of the Three Jewels so that it is never severed. It continues at length to explain that whatever actions they perform are likewise never in vain.
Furthermore, Ratnagotra asked about the characteristics of the pure land:
“What is meant by ‘adorned and purified Buddha-field’?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Cultivating the dedication of merit to the land is the bodhisattva’s pure land.
When the bodhisattva attains bodhi, his realm will be fully adorned with all manner of virtues.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment" states: "Although bodhisattvas may even traverse the five paths of immediate retribution, they possess no heart of malice, affliction, anger, harm, or poison."
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana asked Vimalakīrti about his parents and kin, Vimalakīrti replied:
"The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of a bodhisattva, and skillful means is the father."
"The Mother is the true guide; there is nothing that does not arise from her.
The sixth is wisdom (*prajñā*), the virtue of self-benefit;
the seventh is skillful means (*upāya*), the virtue of benefiting others.
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice," nine million bodhisattvas from the upper direction requested Śākyamuni, saying:
"We pray that you will grant us a small portion of the Dharma, so that we may return to our native land."
The World-Honored One said:
"There is a Dharma-gate of liberation for bodhisattvas called 'Exhaustible and Inexhaustible.
You should practice and study it."
That which is finite is conditioned and subject to arising and ceasing;
that which is called infinite is unconditioned and free from arising and ceasing.
All such merits for one's own benefit are what a bodhisattva should cultivate within.
This is because everything is governed by wisdom.
Fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I have cited only this much regarding the practices for one's own benefit; all other matters should be understood by analogy.

Regarding the practitioner who acts for the benefit of others, it is stated in the "Praise of Virtues" section of the *Introduction Chapter*: "With the sound of the great lion's roar, he expounds the Dharma; his beautiful voice resonates afar, pervading the ten directions. Thus it is extensively explained that all who see or hear him receive benefit."
Later, the elder’s son Ratnākara inquired about the characteristics of purifying Buddha-fields and the manner in which bodhisattvas cultivate Buddha-fields. The World-Honored One replied:
"The realm of all sentient beings is that which constitutes the bodhisattva’s purification of a Buddha-field."
"In accordance with the growth and benefit of all sentient beings, he immediately takes up and purifies Buddha-fields.

In the "Chapter on Skillful Means," the Vimalakīrti is praised, saying: "He is skilled in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), has mastered skillful means (*upāya*), has fulfilled his great vows, and clearly understands the inclinations and conducts of sentient beings."

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment" states: "Although a bodhisattva may travel through the realm of Yama, the Lord of Death, they nevertheless accumulate vast stores of merit and wisdom."
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Universal Manifestation of All Physical Bodies asked Vimalakīrti about his parents and kin, to which Vimalakīrti replied:
"Although I know that all Buddha-fields and sentient beings are empty, I constantly cultivate pure lands and benefit beings without indolence."
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice," the bodhisattvas from the upper regions requested Śākyamuni, saying:
"We pray that you grant us a small portion of the Dharma, so that we may return to our own lands."
The World-Honored One replied:
"What is meant by 'not exhausting the conditioned' (*saṃskṛta*)?
It means that bodhisattvas do not abandon great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and do not relinquish great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)."
What is called the "unexhausted unconditioned"?
Although one contemplates selflessness, one does not abandon great compassion for sentient beings.
This is called the bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned.
Regarding the superior practice of benefiting others, fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I have cited only this much; the remainder may be understood by analogy.
All such meritorious qualities of benefiting others are what a bodhisattva should cultivate externally.

Thus, regarding both ordinary and noble bodhisattvas, whether they have already entered or have not yet entered [the path], a general discussion that encompasses all their characteristics cannot exceed seven stages:

first, the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotrabhūmi*); second, the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*); third, the stage of pure superior intention (*śuddhādhyāśayabhūmi*); fourth, the stage of correct practice (*caryāpratipattibhūmi*); fifth, the stage of certainty (*niyatabhūmi*); sixth, the stage of certain practice (*niyatipratipattibhūmi*); and seventh, the stage of reaching the ultimate (*niṣṭhāgamanabhūmi*).
Within these seven stages, in the first there is the lineage but one is not yet able to practice;
in the next, although one is able to practice, one is not yet able to realize;
in the subsequent stages, although realization is attained in all of them, each succeeding stage is superior to the preceding one.

Furthermore, there are ten stages (*bhūmi*): first, abiding in the lineage (*gotra*); second, having already entered; third, not yet purified in intention and not yet having entered the first stage; fourth, having already purified the intention and having already entered the first stage; fifth, not yet perfected and not yet having reached the ultimate stage; sixth, already perfected and having already reached the ultimate stage; seventh, not yet fallen into certainty and remaining in the state of non-maturation prior to the seventh stage; eighth, already fallen into certainty and abiding in the eighth or ninth stages; ninth, bound to one more birth within the state of reaching the ultimate position; and tenth, the final existence, which is the tenth stage itself.
Although the various practices cultivated by these bodhisattvas are individually infinite, when categorized generally, they do not exceed four types:
first, the practice of the perfections (pāramitā); second, the practice of the bodhisattva stages; third, the practice of the supernormal powers; and fourth, the practice of maturing sentient beings.

Fearing that the text might become too voluminous, I have not been able to detail everything here; it shall be explained separately in the sections below. Accordingly, these internal and external practices should be cultivated.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of births for Bodhisattvas: first, the birth for the removal of calamities.

This refers to how Bodhisattvas, through the power of their great vows and their mastery over supernatural abilities, take birth among species such as giant fish during times of famine and disaster. By making their bodies vast in size, they provide sustenance from within their own bodies to all hungry beings, enabling them to survive with little effort.
Sometimes he holds vidyā-mantras, or acts as a king of medicine to rescue those afflicted by epidemics.
When neighboring countries engage in war and strife, he employs his power to pacify and eliminate them.
When sentient beings are in discord, he admonishes them with words of reconciliation.
Those oppressed by evil rulers are born there as disciplined and compliant beings;
those with wrong views are born in that celestial realm, where they are skillfully led to abandon and sever them.
All such cases are termed "births for the removal of calamities."

Second, birth according to the species: this refers to how bodhisattvas, through the mastery of their great vows, take birth within all various types of beings to serve as leaders, skillfully transforming and guiding them.

He does not himself practice the evils that others practice, and he himself practices the virtues that others do not practice; through skillful means, he exhorts and instructs them to eliminate those faults.

Third is birth with great power (*maheśākhya*), which refers to the fact that when Bodhisattvas are born according to their nature, their lifespan, physical form, lineage, sovereignty, wealth, and other such fruits of maturation (*vipākaphala*) are the most preeminent in all the world.
Fourth, superior birth (*abhyudaya*): this refers to Bodhisattvas who, in the first bhūmi, become a wheel-turning king (*cakravartin*) ruling over Jambudvīpa;
in the second bhūmi, they become a gold-wheel king ruling over the four continents;
and in the third bhūmi, they become a king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
On the fourth bhūmi, one becomes the king of the Yāma devas;
on the fifth bhūmi, the king of the Tuṣita devas;
and on the sixth bhūmi, the king of the Nirmāṇarati devas.
In the seventh stage, one becomes the king of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations;
in the eighth stage, one becomes the king of the first dhyāna heaven;
in the ninth stage, one becomes the king of the second dhyāna heaven.

The Bodhisattva of the tenth stage acts as the Great Sovereign, surpassing the King of the Fourth Dhyāna at Akaniṣṭha; he is the foremost among all places of birth. He avoids the Heaven of the Four Great Kings because they lack a fixed ruler;
he avoids the Third Dhyāna because it is the ultimate pleasure of the world.

The five most excellent births refer to those bodhisattvas whose accumulations for enlightenment are already fully perfected, who are born into the family of brahmins, the family of great state preceptors, or the family of kṣatriyas of great royal houses, and are able to manifest equal enlightenment and extensively perform the deeds of a Buddha; this shall be analyzed in detail in the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.
In accordance with Vimalakīrti, among these five types of births, he possesses immeasurable wealth and resources to support the destitute; thus, it is called the "birth for the removal of calamities.
If he appears as a householder, he is honored among householders and excels in preaching the Dharma; thus, it is called the "birth according to the class."

Having already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas and deeply planted the roots of virtue, because the cause is so great, the fruit is likewise not small; thus he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta (Great Power Born).
Since he does not currently undergo the retribution of the Ten Kings, this is not a case of "superior birth" (*abhyudaya-janman*).
Because they do not possess the marks of a Bodhisattva in his final existence, they are not in their last birth.
Alternatively, they are merely those born according to the species, who encompass all classes of beings as leaders in order to transform them all.
All of this arises because Bodhisattvas practice both internal and external cultivation for their own benefit and the benefit of others; thus they are able to manifest this.
It is because Bodhisattvas possess such qualities and take such births that they carry out deeds of benefit.
In the subsequent section of this sutra, the "Chapter on the Fragrant Terrace," Vimalakīrti says to the bodhisattvas from the upper direction:
"O Great Beings, Śākyamuni Tathāgata performs what is difficult to do;
concealing his immeasurable, noble, and majestic virtues, he does not shrink from toil as he employs skillful means to subdue sentient beings who are stubborn and fierce."

The bodhisattvas among the sentient beings of this land are likewise able to endure various forms of toil and fatigue; they accomplish steadfast great compassion and vigor, supporting and propagating the unsurpassed True Dharma of the Tathāgata to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.

The merit obtained by practicing the bodhisattva path for a single lifetime to benefit sentient beings in this Sahā world is greater than the merit gained from practicing the bodhisattva path to bring benefit and happiness for hundreds of thousands of great eons in the world of Exquisite Fragrance.
Because there are ten ways of practicing wholesome dharmas in this world—namely, gathering the poor through generosity, up to gathering sentient beings through the four means of integration.

Although it is known that all bodhisattvas cultivate both internal and external practices, this sutra is intended to reveal that the bodhisattvas of this land cultivate inconceivable and superior practices that excel those of other buddha-fields.

Fourth, to manifest the great majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata: although the holy virtues of the Buddhas are hundreds of thousands in number, when categorized by type, they do not exceed two kinds:
first, great majestic power; second, great spiritual virtue.

There are three kinds of power: first, the power of the noble ones (*ārya-vaśitā*); second, the power of the Dharma (*dharma-vaśitā*); and third, innate power (*sahaja-vaśitā*). Regarding the power of the noble ones:

it refers to the Buddha’s cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in the past, whereby he now attains mastery over concentration based upon that practice. All things are accomplished according to his wishes because of his pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and his well-cultivated mind; thus, it is called the power of the noble ones.

The power of the Dharma refers to the fact that when a bodhisattva in the past cultivated the six perfections and other such sublime dharmas, there were vast fruits and great benefits; this is called the power of the Dharma.

Regarding "innate power" (*sahaja-prabhāva*): it refers to the fact that the Buddha, having previously accumulated a vast store of merit and provisions over many eons, realized an exceedingly marvelous dharma that is innate; this is called innate power.

The first is the power of the noble ones (*ārya-prabhāva*), which consists of the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*): first, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the power of the basis of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*);

second, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*); third, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*); fourth, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the power of seeing death and rebirth (*cyuty-upapāda-darśana-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*); fifth, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the power of knowing the diversity of minds (*cetaḥ-paryāya-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*); and sixth, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*).
First, the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*) has two aspects:
first, the power of transformation (*pariṇāmika*), and second, the power of creation (*nairmāṇika*).
"Transformation" refers to altering that which previously existed; it consists of the eighteen transformations:

1. Trembling; 2. Blazing; 3. Pervading; 4. Manifesting; 5. Transforming; 6. Coming and going; 7. Contracting; 8. Expanding; 9. Entering all forms into one’s own body; 10. Traveling to similar realms; 11. Making visible; 12. Concealing; 13. Mastery over what is created; 14. Restraining the supernatural powers of others; 15. Bestowing eloquence; 16. Bestowing mindfulness; 17. Bestowing peace and happiness; 18. Emitting great radiance.
"Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) refers to that which did not previously exist but now exists; it consists of three types:
transformation of body, transformation of environment, and transformation of speech.
As stated above regarding the two kinds of transformation, they are capable of performing two functions:
First, they lead all sentient beings into the Buddha’s holy teaching; second, they bestow gifts upon immeasurable sentient beings who are suffering.

The supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the Śrāvakas reach only up to two thousand worlds, while those of the Pratyekabuddhas can reach three thousand worlds; however, the Tathāgata’s supernatural powers can pervade the ten directions in a single moment of thought.

From the first stage (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva up to the hundred buddha-worlds, and so on until the tenth stage, according to the number of their respective categories, the limits are as described in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, extending even to the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).

The followers of the two vehicles are only able to sever the seeds and manifest forms of the outflows (*āsrava*), but they do not sever the *dausthulya* (coarse heaviness). They know for themselves that their outflows are exhausted, yet they do not know others or the means for exhausting outflows; nor do they know that others may harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*) regarding the exhaustion of outflows.

The Tathāgata has completely severed all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of both the seeds and their manifestations; he is able to know the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) in himself and others, as well as the means for such exhaustion. Furthermore, he can recognize when others possess overweening pride (*adhimāna*), while remaining himself free from defilement; he is also skilled at extensively analyzing and explaining various forms of overweening pride for the sake of others.

Regarding these six kinds of supernormal transformations just mentioned, the "Introduction Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) of this sutra states: "Five hundred precious natures offered parasols; the Buddha merged them into one, which completely covered the great trichiliocosm."
This is the fifth transformation among the eight subsequent transformations, because it transforms the many into one;
it is also the eighth expansion, because it expands the small into the great.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the great assembly harbored doubts in their hearts, pressed this great earth with his toe; immediately, the trichiliocosm was adorned with immeasurable thousands of wondrous jewels, which was also subsumed under the fifth transformation.

To speak according to reality, what the Bodhisattvas perceive is fundamentally a pure land, whereas the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings perceive it as an impure land. Now, for the sake of the Śrāvakas and others, this impure region is transformed into a pure land; therefore, this is subsumed under the fifth transformation.
The reverse process—transforming it back into an impure land—is likewise so, because such transformations are possible through the Buddha’s sovereign resolve (*adhimukti*).

In the "Chapter on Inquiring after the Illness," at that time, Vimalakīrti, by means of his great supernatural power, caused his room to become empty, removing all possessions except for a single couch, upon which he manifested himself lying ill.
This refers to the twelfth of the eighteen transformations, "concealment," because it causes all things to vanish and become invisible.
In the "Inconceivable" chapter, Śāriputra desired a seat, but was rebuked and told to do so for the sake of the Dharma. Subsequently, Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī:
"In which buddha-field are there jeweled seats?"
Mañjuśrī said:
"To the east, thirty-six Ganges-sands of Buddha-fields away from here, there is a Buddha-world named Mountain Banner; the Buddha there is named Mountain Lamp King."
The body of the Buddha was eighty-four billion *yojana*s in height, and his lion throne was sixty-eight billion *yojana*s high.
The body of the Bodhisattva was forty-two billion *yojana*s in height, and his throne was thirty-four billion *yojana*s high.
"It is most excellent.
Then, Vimalakīrti manifested great supernormal powers, and the Buddha King of Mountain Lamps sent thirty-two billion grand lion thrones to enter his room.
Among the eighteen transformations, this is the sixth dwelling;
it is also the thirteenth, the mastery of action, wherein by the power of mindfulness, things arrive as soon as they are thought of, because one has attained sovereignty.
Thus, the chamber of Vimalakīrti suddenly became vast, magnificent, and pure.

"Vast and expansive" refers to the eighth transformation of extension; because it transforms the small into the great, it is able to entirely encompass thirty-two billion lion thrones without any mutual obstruction.

The great city of Vaiśālī, and even the palaces inhabited by the asuras and others, were not cramped; all were seen exactly as they were before, without any difference between the former and the latter.
This is the ninth [manifestation]: the entry of various images into the body. The images did not become small, nor did the body become large; therefore, this is what is subsumed here.
Because the body is the primary factor, it is called the "body" (*kāya*).
This is subsumed under the metaphor of a great image entering a small room.
He caused each of the bodhisattvas to transform their own bodies to the size of forty-two billion *yojanas* and ascend the lion thrones.
This is the eighth expansion, for it expands the small into the great.
Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra:
"The dwelling of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in liberation is called inconceivable."
"One is able to place Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, within a mustard seed; to place the four great oceans within a single pore; and to place a trichiliocosm within the palm of one's hand.
Regarding these three types [of miracles], both the large and small dimensions remain without increase or decrease; this is precisely what is meant by "these various forms entering the body."
Alternatively, seven days may be regarded as one kalpa; this is the eighth mode of expansion, wherein the short is made long.
Alternatively, one kalpa may be compressed into seven days; this is the seventh mode of contraction, wherein the long is made short.

All such abidings in liberation through the inconceivable spiritual power of the Buddha are explained in detail below; they are all subsumed within the three types of transformations among the eighteen miraculous manifestations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*).

In the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings," the celestial maidens scatter flowers; these flowers are the manifested objects (*nirmāṇa-viṣaya*) produced through the supernormal power of the knowledge of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna-abhijñā*), for they are transformed into fragrance and so forth.
Among the eight rare wonders, the first marvel states: "This chamber is constantly filled with golden light," which refers to the eighteenth transformation: the emission of great radiance.

Even up to the eighth [topic], "In this chamber, the meritorious adornments of all buddha-fields and the exquisite, wondrous decorations of the palaces of the devas are constantly manifested," this too is subsumed under this very transformation, or it may also be the entry of various images into the body.

In the "Chapter on the Fragrant Terrace" (Gandhakūṭa-parivarta), he transformed himself into a bodhisattva and ascended to the Fragrant Realm (Gandhavatī) to invite the Buddha for a meal; together with nine million bodhisattvas, they all came here—this was the sixth round of coming and going.

The fact that the entire assembly witnessed the Bodhisattva’s journey to those places is subsumed under the fourth manifestation (*nirmāṇa*), because he manifested those events so that the assembly might see them.
The transformation of nine million seats and so forth constitutes the realm of transformation (*nirmāṇa-viṣaya*), as these things came into being where they previously did not exist.
When the great assembly has eaten their rice and there is still a remainder, this too is "expansive" (*śū*), for it expands the small to become much.
Thus, the extensive exposition of the deeds of Akṣobhya Buddha is all subsumed herein; each subsequent point shall be individually correlated as appropriate.
All that has been explained above consists of the power of the noble ones' supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*) and, next, the power of the Dharma.
By virtue of the "blade" of power from the Bodhisattva’s past cultivation of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), four aspects are accomplished:
first, the severing of hindrances; second, the accomplishment of the provisions (*saṃbhāra*); third, the benefiting of oneself and others; and fourth, the bestowing of future fruits.

Through giving, one is able to sever stinginess; it serves as one's own provision for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), and it can also eliminate the manifold sufferings of others—such as hunger, thirst, illness, and deprivation. Furthermore, it brings about future wealth and happiness, as well as the attainment of great rank, riches, and a vast circle of followers.

Furthermore, by means of wisdom, one is able to sever ignorance and take it as one's own provision; through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), one brings sentient beings to maturity; by awakening to objects as they truly are, one induces great pure joy; and for the sake of all sentient beings, one preaches the Dharma in accordance with reason, causing them to obtain benefit and happiness in both the present and the future.
Gathering all roots of goodness and being able to correctly perform what is to be done, one shall realize in the future the dissociation from the two obstacles.

These are sequentially assigned to the four characteristics of the world: stinginess and ignorance are entirely severed, extending even to rank, wealth, factions, and kin; because one gathers all roots of goodness, there is the realization of dissociation from the two [obstacles].
This demonstrates the power of wholesome dharmas.

Subsequently, there is the power of co-arising: namely, the natural capacity to remember various events from previous births; acting spontaneously with a resolute mind; being able to endure great suffering; and only passing away after exhausting the full lifespan of the Tuṣita Heaven.
His lifespan, physical form, and renown surpass those [of others]; descending to be born, he enters the womb while emitting light that shines afar.
During the three stages of entering, abiding, and emerging from the womb, he possesses correct awareness.
Upon birth, he took seven steps without waiting for support.

Devas and nāgas of majestic power scattered incense as an offering; his body was adorned with the primary and secondary marks, and he utterly destroyed the malevolent forces of Māra. Every limb and joint was endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
From childhood, he naturally attained mastery in the arts; without a teacher, he was able to realize unsurpassed *bodhi*. The Great Brahma Heaven King spontaneously exhorted him.
Though thunder and lightning struck with terror, he remained unmoved in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), causing even the crawling insects to turn toward him in faith as Bodhisattvas.

Once he had attained Buddhahood, even those as low as the animals came to make offerings; clouds and dragons constantly waited upon him, raining whenever he bathed and failing to fall while he was walking.
When he sat, the branches and twigs of the trees all bent their shadows downward, shading his body in accordance with his movements, never failing or withdrawing.
For six years, Māra sought an opportunity [to harm him] but could not find one.

Those with leprosy and epilepsy were freed from their delusory visions and returned to their original states of mind; those with inverted fetuses became normal, the blind regained their sight, and the deaf regained their hearing.
The three poisons were eliminated; he always lay on his right side, remaining undisturbed even when resting upon grass mats or similar bedding, and though appearing to sleep, he did not turn over.
The wind could not move his robes; he walked like a lion and stepped like a bull king, first lifting the right foot and only then shifting the left.
The ground should follow the natural contours of the terrain, being free of gravel and stones; the gates should be proportionate in size; and food should be broken into small morsels before eating.
At the time of Parinirvāṇa, the great earth trembled, and the myriad stars shone brilliantly as they intermingled.
Such matters as these are termed "innate majestic power" (*sahaja-prabhāva*) and are not produced by the majestic power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*).

This sutra sets forth in detail the majestic powers of the five Buddhas—Gandhakūṭa, Dīparāja, Akṣobhya, Bhaiṣajyarāja, and Śākyamuni; for the others, it is stated according to what is appropriate, whether they possess them or not, as their specific deeds cannot be fully revealed here in advance. They shall be extensively indicated in the subsequent sections of the text.

The "Great Sage’s Virtue" refers to the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s perfection of the ten titles, as well as the two abandonments and the two knowledges; this is termed the Great Sage’s Virtue. Regarding the two abandonments:

they refer to the abandonment of the habitual tendencies of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the abandonment of the habitual tendencies of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). These are the true principles manifested when the two obstructions are exhausted. Because they are manifested through the abandonment of obstructions and possess the nature of abandonment, they are called "abandonment."
Regarding the two types of wisdom: having severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the non-conforming wisdom is the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Having severed the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the unobstructed wisdom regarding all objects is the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Furthermore, three types of wisdom may be described: namely, pure wisdom (*viśuddha-jñāna*), all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajña-jñāna*), and unimpeded wisdom (*apratihata-jñāna*).

Moreover, there are the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), namely: the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*), the eighty secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*), the four kinds of purity in every respect (*sarvākāra-viśuddhi*), the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the ten powers (*bala*), the three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*), the three ways in which he needs no protection (*arakṣya*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the quality of never forgetting (*asaṃpramoṣadharman*), the permanent destruction of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-samudghāta*), the sublime wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākāra-prajñā*), as well as the Buddha’s absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and so forth—all such things are termed the dharmas of the Great Sage’s virtues.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicles 48 and 49, elucidates the distinctions between the essence and the meaning of these merits,
so too does this present sutra reveal that the Buddha possesses seven kinds of supremacy, which are termed "the Great Holy Virtues" (*mahāryaguṇa*).
First is the excellence of the basis, which reveals that the Buddha’s body possesses the various marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

Second is the excellence of correct practice, whereby through the Buddha’s two benefits—benefiting and bringing peace and happiness, and having compassion for the world—he causes all devas and humans to obtain their welfare and benefit.
Third is the excellence of perfection, meaning that the Buddha’s four qualities—ethical discipline, view, conduct, and pure livelihood—are all complete.
Fourth is the excellence of wisdom, because the Buddha has fully accomplished the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Fifth is superiority in power, because of possessing the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Sixth is superiority in abandonment, because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of both obstacles are forever severed.
Seventh is superiority in abiding, because one frequently dwells in the three superior abidings—namely, the noble, celestial, and Brahma abidings—which are unsurpassed.
The three gates of liberation and the meditative attainment of cessation are called the noble abodes (*āryavihāra*).
Frequent dwelling in the meditative attainment of cessation and the four dhyānas is called the celestial abode (*devavihāra*).
Frequent dwelling in the immovable fourth dhyāna and the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) is called the Brahma abode (*brahmavihāra*).

Abiding extensively in great compassion, he observes the world day and night during the six periods with his Buddha-eye to discern who is increasing or decreasing in roots of goodness, and who has attained the three vehicles.
This sutra, from beginning to end, reveals these seven excellences, which are termed the "Great Holy Virtues.
Together with the accomplishment of power and holy majesty, they are collectively named the fourth: the Tathāgata’s Majestic Virtue.

Fifth, regarding those whose faculties have matured and who are suitable to hear [the teaching] at a given time: with the eye of great compassionate wisdom, the Buddha observes all worlds throughout the six periods of day and night; through his skillful means and beneficial actions, he is free from the four faults.
First, there is no improper place; second, no improper time; third, no improper dharma; and fourth, no unsuitable vessel.
How much more so in this sutra, which says: "In all the majestic deportment and movements of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, whatever they perform is nothing other than a Buddha-activity."
Therefore, when this sutra is preached, it is appropriate for the assembly to hear it; it is not a vain bestowal that brings no benefit to the listeners.
This sutra contains thirteen stages of benefit in total.

First, in the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta), because the marks of the Buddha-land’s adornment and purity were explained, five hundred sons of elders attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Eighty-four thousand people all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
thirty-two thousand people, realizing that conditioned phenomena are impermanent, became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye;
and eight thousand bhikṣus attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows.

In the "Chapter on Expedient Means," Vimalakīrti manifested illness; when questioned regarding the teaching of the Dharma, countless thousands of people all resolved their minds upon unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Within the two chapters on the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas, although each attained awakening upon first encountering Vimalakīrti at that time, they were sent away without reporting to the Buddha that they had attained the Way.

In the "Chapter on Inquiring after Illness," through their mutual discourse, eight thousand devaputras all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

In the "Chapter on the Inconceivable," Mahākāśyapa used the metaphor of a person born blind to illustrate his lack of understanding regarding the dharma-gate of liberation; consequently, thirty-two thousand devaputras all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and eight thousand bodhisattvas attained entry into the power of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of bodhisattvas, entering the inconceivable realm of liberation.
In the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" and the "Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment," the attainment of the Way is not mentioned.
In the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality," five thousand bodhisattvas all entered the dharma-gate of non-duality.

In the "Chapter on the Fragrant Terrace," it is taught that ten matters surpass those of other buddha-fields; by accomplishing eight dharmas, one is born in a pure land. Five thousand devaputras all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice," nine million bodhisattvas from the upper direction, having heard the Dharma of the exhaustible and the inexhaustible, rejoiced. They scattered exquisite fragrant flowers over the great trichiliocosm to make offerings to the Buddha-dharma and the bodhisattvas; thereafter, they suddenly vanished and returned to their own land.

In the "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata," because they beheld Akṣobhya Tathāgata in the world-system of Abhirati, ten nayutas of people all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and vowed to be reborn in that realm; the Buddha then prophesied their future birth there.
The "Dharma-Offering Chapter" (*Dharmapūjā-parivarta*) and the "Entrustment Chapter" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) do not speak of attaining the Way.

Second, regarding the fundamental tenets of the sutras: the former masters of this land, relying on the doctrinal principles found in the extant sutras and śāstras, have established four schools in total:
first, the School of Establishing Nature (*Lìxìng-zōng*).

The Sarvāstivāda school, including works such as the *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya*, and the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, maintains that all phenomena established within the three categories possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Second is the school that refutes intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
It holds that while all phenomena possess characteristics, they are entirely devoid of real intrinsic nature.
This school refutes the previous position of establishing intrinsic nature; the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) belongs to this category.
Third is the School that Shatters Characteristics (Poxiangzong).

Not only are intrinsic natures empty, but the characteristic marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) are also not truly existent. This includes the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and treatises such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*.
Fourth is the school that reveals reality (*tattvavāda*).

It elucidates the true principle of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), according to which they are either empty or existent as appropriate. The *Nirvāṇa*, *Avataṃsaka*, and *Laṅkāvatāra* sūtras belong to this category.
If the sūtras and śāstras were limited to only this much, one could definitively establish four schools.
For instance, the old *Āgama-sūtra* states: "When Śāriputra entered nirvāṇa, the gods of the formless realm shed tears like a fine spring rain."
As for the Mahāsāṃghika sūtras, under which school are they subsumed?
The *Brahmajāla-sūtra on the Sixty-two Views* and the *Śāriputrābhidharma* belong to the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school.
The *Sammitīya-śāstra* is a treatise of the Sthavira school.
Since such scriptures and treatises do not belong to the four schools, how can you claim that there are only four schools in total?
Now, based on the newly translated sūtras and śāstras, and relying generally upon all the teachings, there are three categories of teaching;
when the fundamental tenets are established through reasoning, there are eight such tenets.

Regarding the three categories of teaching: in the second fascicle of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the World-Honored One extensively expounded for the Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata that, because the essence and characteristics of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) do not exist, it is called the "naturelessness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

Because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) lacks the self-arising of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is said to have the "nature of non-nature in terms of arising" (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*);
because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) lacks the imagined nature, it is said to have the "ultimate nature of non-nature" (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The three natures were explained as all being based on the non-existence of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Having already caused Paramārthasamudgata to gain deep understanding, and having extensively taught the analogies of worldly *viśvabhaṣaja* medicine, a variegated painting, and clarified butter and space, the Blessed One praised him for his excellent comprehension of what had been said.
The Bodhisattva Paramārthasamudgata again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, at one time in the past, while staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana, you turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma by means of the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths solely for those who had set out on the Vehicle of the Śrāvakas."
Although this is most marvelous and extremely rare, among all the gods and humans in the world, none previously had been able to turn it according to the Dharma.
Yet the wheel of Dharma turned at that time was subject to superior [teachings] and possessed room for further development; it was of provisional meaning and served as a basis for various disputes.

In the past, during the second period, the Bhagavān turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma by means of the hidden mode of teaching, solely for those who had set out upon the Mahāyāna path, based on the fact that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are without arising or ceasing, are primordially quiescent, and are by nature in a state of nirvāṇa.

Although it was even more marvelous and exceedingly rare, the wheel of Dharma turned at that time was still surpassable, subject to further interpretation, of provisional meaning, and a basis for various disputes.

Now, during this third period, the World-Honored One has turned the wheel of the sublime Dharma for those who have set out upon all vehicles, based on the fact that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, are without arising or ceasing, are quiescent from the beginning, and are by nature in nirvāṇa—by means of the characteristic of manifest clarity; this is supremely marvelous and most rare.
"The wheel of Dharma now turned by the World-Honored One is unsurpassed and unassailable; it is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), not a basis for various disputes.
This refers to the three kinds of wheels of Dharma—turning, illuminating, and sustaining—as taught in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

The World-Honored One’s initial teaching on the Four Noble Truths as practiced by those of the three vehicles is called the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma; it alone receives the name "turning" because it proceeds through twelve aspects.
During the second period, he taught the Mahāyāna doctrine of the exclusive principle of emptiness; because this illumination shatters existence, it is called the Illuminating Wheel of Dharma.

The teaching of the third period expounds the emptiness that dispels what is grasped and preserves the existence of the two natures; it is suitable for practitioners of all three vehicles to cultivate and maintain, and is thus called the "Wheel of Dharma.
